gloss: i.e. would that that voice had sounded. *he who*, St John. See Rev. xii. 12, “Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath.” *Apocalypse*, revelation, ‘uncovering.’
i.e. the tempter before he was the accuser. Cf. Rev. xii. 10, “the accuser of our brethren is cast down.”

i.e. rouses the memory of what he was and the thought of what he is and will be. So Samson is beset by thoughts of “Times past, what once I was, and what am now.” In both passages the influence is clear of Dante’s famous words: “There is no greater pain than to recall a happy time in wretchedness.”
pondering many things (*multa volvens*). The speech that follows throws much light on Milton’s conception of Satan.
The lines written as early as 1642. Addison considered this speech (32–113) “the finest ascribed to Satan in the whole poem.”

lemma: whom he created what I was
gloss: in bk. V. when he is inciting the angels to rebel Satan pretends that he and they are “self-begot, self-raised,” i.e. not created by the Almighty and so not justly his servants.
disdained. *quit*, pay off, settle.
i.e. disdain forbids me (to use) that word “submission.”
doing penance, asking pardon (cf. Fr. *grâce*).
just as evil is to be his good, so later (IX. 122, 123) he confesses, “all good to me becomes Bane” (i.e. evil).

i.e. each of the three passions—anger, envy, despair—dimmed his face which was three times changed with the paleness caused by them. Cf. such expressions as ‘pale with anger,’ ‘pale with envy.’ *pale* = paleness.

Masson says: “Eden is the whole tract or district of Western Asia wherein the Creator has designed that men should first dwell; Paradise is the Happy Garden situated in one particular spot of this Eden—on its eastern side.” *Paradise*, ‘a park’; a word of Persian origin.

an open, level summit of open land. The garden occupies a plateau or table-land, circular in shape and surrounded by a grassy mound or wall. This idea of setting the Garden on the summit of a hill is traced to Ezekiel xxviii. 13, 14.
*ranks*; like the ascending tiers of seats in an amphitheatre. Perhaps Vallombrosa was in Milton’s thoughts.
“The fragrance thus wafted out to sea, sometimes to a distance of twenty or more miles, is well known to every sailor who has been in the West Indies or in the Indian Archipelago” (Keightley).

more commonly Mozambique; a Portuguese province on the east coast of Africa, opposite Madagascar. *Sabean*, of or from Saba = Sheba. *Araby the Blest* = Lat. *Arabia Felix*, each epithet indicating the fertility of the region.

*Asmodeus*, one of the rebellious angels expelled from Heaven. The angel Raphael bade Tobias marry a Jewish maiden, Sara. Her seven husbands had been destroyed in succession by Asmodeus who was in love with her. Tobias was instructed by Raphael to burn the heart and liver of a fish, since the smell would drive away the spirit.

one of Milton’s prose-works was a treatise on “The Likeliest Means to remove Hirelings out of the Church” (1659). It seemed to him wrong that ministers of religion should receive salaries. We must remember that he speaks as an enemy, a bitter enemy, of the English Church. *lewd*, base.
i.e. in the shape of a cormorant, chosen because a ravenous bird of prey and thus symbolical of Satan himself.

what use could Satan have made of the tree? He was already immortal. Perhaps M. means that if Satan had eaten of the tree’s fruit its saving power might have given him true life—a regeneration of spirit that, leading to repentance, would have enabled him to regain his true archangelic immortality.
according to these limits, which indicate, however, only its eastern and western points, Eden lay in Syria and Mesopotamia—mainly in the latter.

long the capital of Western Asia; on the right bank of the Tigris, about 20 miles S.E. of the modern Bagdad. It was built by Seleucus, a Macedonian who became one of Alexander’s generals, and about 312 B.C. founded the dynasty of the Seleucidæ, kings of Syria.

The river flowing through Eden reaches the hill on the level summit of which is Paradise. Part of the river goes straight through by a subterranean passage and issues in the plain on the other side. But part of its water is drawn up through the hill to the surface in the form of a fountain.
*sapphire*, sapphire-coloured, i.e. light blue. *fount*, source. *crisped*, rippling; often used of wind ruffling the surface of water. *error*, in the literal sense of Lat. *error*, ‘a wandering.’
“the stories told of the apples of the Hesperides being true only of this place, if at all.” It is an absolute clause in parenthesis.

part of the curse (Genesis iii. 18) was that the earth should bring forth thorns and thistles; hence the presumption that there were no thorns before Adam’s sin (Newton). Thyer quotes Herrick: “Before man’s fall the rose was born, Saint Ambrose says, without a thorn.”

An allegorical way of saying, with classical imagery, that in Eden only one season was known, viz. spring. *Pan*; here regarded as the god of all nature, and called “universal” in allusion to his name. *Graces*, three goddesses who personified the refinements and elevated joys of life. *Hours*, goddesses personifying the seasons of the year.

according to the classical legend, Proserpine was carried off by Pluto = Dis, to the nether world, unknown to her mother Ceres, and became his wife. Latin poets made Enna in Sicily the scene of the incident, the worship of Ceres having been introduced into Rome from Sicily.

“Near the city of Antioch, on the Orontes, lay a grove sacred to Apollo, in which was a temple of the god, whence he gave oracles. It was named Daphne, and a spring which watered it was called the Castalian spring, after that at Delphi” (Keightley).

Abyssinian. *Amara*; correctly Amhara; it is rather a range of hills than a single “mount.” Todd quotes Heylin: “the hill of Amara is a day’s journey high, on the top whereof are thirty-four palaces in which the younger sons of the Emperor are continually enclosed to avoid sedition.”

the repetition of “erect” is important, since M. treats man’s stature as a symbol of his sovereignty over the “prone” beast-creation. M. “drew the portrait of Adam not without regard to his own person, of which he had no mean opinion” (Newton).

This relation of woman to man—“not equal”—runs throughout the scenes in which Adam and Eve are introduced. Such lines as these express Milton’s personal conception of woman’s status and capacities; and how much it differed from modern views may be illustrated by the single fact that his treatise *On Education* makes no reference to the education of women.
*hyacinthine*; a classical epithet. A dark colour, perhaps deep brown, seems implied. Milton’s own hair was auburn; the Bodleian Library has a lock of it, considered genuine.
M. often uses this classical figure of speech called oxymoron by which two words connoting opposite ideas are closely associated.

a famous example of an idiom often used by Elizabethan, as it had been by Greek, writers. It combines the comparative and superlative constructions—thus: ‘Eve fair*er* than all her daughters’ + ‘Eve fair*est* of all women.’

winding himself into folds (Lat. *sinus*). *Gordian twine*, intricate tangle. *his braided train*, his twisted, interlaced tail. “That intricate form into which he put himself was a sort of symbol or type of his fraud, though not then regarded” (Richardson).

i.e. in the Atlantic, in which, according to the classical fancy, the sun set. *ascending scale*; to be taken, I think, not literally as a reference to an astronomical fact or theory, but merely as a metaphor for the alternations of day and night.
considering how happy they are: their security is not in proportion to their happiness.
‘Public reason—viz. honour and empire—compels.’ So in *S. A.* 865–70 Dalila excuses her treachery to Samson on the ground that “the public good” of her country required it.
perhaps an allusion to Charles’s plea for ship-money (Newton). Cromwell pleaded the same excuse for the execution of Charles.
there is, I think, an almost quibbling use of *sole*—(1) ‘only,’ (2) ‘unique’ (implying ‘chief’). Eve is the only sharer in Adam’s joys—and herself the chief element of them.
*one*, emphatic by position; ‘only one.’ *easy*, to keep (but also to break); an unconscious irony.
M. had in mind Ovid’s story of Narcissus, *Metamorphoses* III. 407 et seq.
the name Eve is thought to mean ‘life.’
in the literal sense ‘not to be divided,’ inseparable; Lat. *individuus*. So Horace calls Mæcenas *meæ partem animæ* and Vergil *animæ dimidium meæ*.
used by other writers of the 17th century. Dante has it in the *Paradiso*, XXVIII. 3.
it is a chance, just a possibility, that chance may lead, etc.: the grim sort of quibble in which bitterness (here jealousy) finds vent.

‘man of God’; one of the seven great Spirits. Following, no doubt, some tradition, M. makes him in *P. L.* one of the chief warriors of the Heavenly host, though inferior to Michael. In the Bible Gabriel is always a peaceful intermediary between Heaven and Earth and the bearer of tidings to man.
when M. speaks of the offices assigned to the Heavenly beings he seems to have in his mind the Temple-service of the Jews and the distribution of the Levites “by lot,” 1 Chronicles xxiii.–xxv.

he will not decide whether the sun had revolved to the west or the Earth to the east, i.e. whether the Ptolemaic astronomy or the Copernican is right. For the general purposes of his poem M. accepts the old Ptolemaic system, but he lets the reader see that he knows the Copernican. *prime orb*, surely the sun.
song with variations.
A striking example of the poetic artifice called epanadiplosis or ‘repetition.’ The passage illustrates well Milton’s love of Nature.
A reference to current astrology.
i.e. into watches; literally = the Latin phrase *dividere noctem* used of Roman soldiers marking the watches of the night by sounding on a trumpet the signal for relieving guard.

*Sylvanus*, a Latin divinity of the fields and woods (Lat. *silva*, wood), much the same as *Faunus*, the god of fields and shepherds, or the Greek Pan, god of flocks and pastoral life. The three deities were often identified.

to benefit mankind, Prometheus (‘fore-thought’) stole the fire of Zeus (Jove); Zeus in revenge caused Hephaestus (Vulcan) to make a woman out of earth who should bring misery on mankind. She was called Pandora or All-gifted. Hermes conducted her to Epimetheus (‘after-thought’), “the unwiser son”; and he married her.
*Japhet*, one of the Titans, father of Prometheus and Epimetheus. Apparently M. identifies him with the Japhet of Scripture.
in *The Christian Doctrine*, II. 4, M. says, “No particular posture of the body in prayer was enjoined, even under the law.” He makes Adam and Eve sometimes stand, sometimes kneel, when they pray.
M. often shows his dislike of ceremonies and forms in worship.
the allusion is to monachism and the celibacy of priests.
according to legend, “winged Cupid,” the god of love, had two sorts of arrows, one tipped with gold to inspire love, the other with lead to repel love (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I. 468–71).
probably M. is glancing particularly at the dissolute court of Charles II.

the Puritans greatly disliked the practice of men and women dancing together. *mask*, a private form of theatrical entertainment, the forerunner of the opera. He himself wrote a mask in *Comus*, 1634; but the Milton of *Paradise Lost*, 1667, was a very different person.
M. has borrowed the Greek phrases ‘on the shield side, i.e. to the left,’ and ‘to the spear side, i.e. to the right.’ The military terms suit the context and lend dignity.
*Ithuriel*, ‘the discovery of God.’ *Zephon*, ‘a looking out.’ The names suit the duty which Gabriel assigns to these two Cherubim.
Pope has an effective allusion to this line in the famous satire on ‘Sporus’ (Lord Hervey), *Epistle to Arbuthnot*.

“Tennyson used to say that the two grandest of all Similes were those of the Ships hanging in the Air, and ‘the Gunpowder one,’ which he used slowly and grimly to enact” (Edward Fitzgerald). Nitre or saltpetre is an ingredient of gunpowder.
*against*, in preparation for. Various battle-touches in *P. L.* (especially in bk. VI.) seem like a reminiscence of the Civil War.

lemma: Virtue in her shape how lovely
gloss: *shape* = Lat. *forma* in its philosophical sense ‘outward manifestation’; cf. *forma honesti*—‘shape of virtue,’ Cicero, *De Officiis* I. 5. 15.
Gabriel, belonging to one of the highest of the Heavenly Orders, has known Satan (an archangel) in the past, and so recognises him here; Zephon, an inferior angel, did not.
Lat. *dolor*, ‘pain.’
either (1) ‘I withstood, resisted, thy fiercest attack’; or (2) ‘I proved myself (“stood”) thy fiercest foe.’ The first way, which makes *stood* transitive, is preferable.

lemma: on earth, or in mid air
gloss: an allusion to the Rabbinical view, commonly adopted by mediæval writers, that the angels who fell with Satan were the same as the spirits or “dæmons” who inhabited the “elements” of earth and air.

in these lines Gabriel speaks to the host of Satan’s followers, as though they were present; *your* refers to them—not, of course, to Satan, whom Gabriel addresses as *thou*. In Shakespeare *thou* is often a contemptuous form of address.
i.e. the close array of angels spread itself out in the shape of a crescent moon. *phalanx*, battalion.

i.e. “with their spears held in their hands across their breasts and slanting beyond the left shoulder, ready to be brought down to the ‘charge’ if necessary” (Masson). “Port” is really a military term.

the general idea of the “golden scales” of the Almighty is from Homer, *Iliad* VIII. 69–72. He identifies the Scales with the sign of the Zodiac called Libra—‘the Balance’—a poetic fancy which gives at once a certain reality to the fiction of the Scales and a new association and interest to Libra itself.

only Satan himself is weighed. The one weight represents the consequence (= “sequel”) to Satan of fighting, the other the consequence of departing: the scale containing the weight that symbolises fighting shows, by its ascent, that Satan’s chance of success is light—weighed and found wanting.
i.e. nor said more. This omission of verbs of saying is common in Vergil, whose influence on M. was so great.
